questions.context: Tom has toothache. He says: "I need to see ___ dentist today, but I don't know which one yet."
questions.instruction: Fill in the blank with the correct article.
questions.explanation: The dentist is not yet specific, so we introduce any one of many dentists with 'a'.

commonWrongAnswers.comment: It's tempting because 'dentist' feels familiar, but Tom hasn't chosen a particular one yet.
You use 'an' before a vowel sound, but 'dentist' starts with a consonant sound.

questions.context: At the clinic yesterday, the nurse said to me: "I will check your blood pressure after lunch." Now I tell my mother: "The nurse said she ___ check my blood pressure after lunch."
questions.instruction: Fill in the blank with one word.
questions.explanation: In reported speech about the past, 'will' changes to 'would' after 'said'.

commonWrongAnswers.comment: The nurse spoke yesterday, so in reported speech 'will' usually shifts back to 'would'.
'Could' means ability or possibility, but the nurse originally promised with 'will'.

questions.context: I am going to the gym every morning before work.
questions.correctAnswer: I go to the gym every morning before work.
questions.explanation: A regular habit with 'every morning' takes the present simple, so it's 'I go'.

commonWrongAnswers.answer: I went to the gym every morning before work.
commonWrongAnswers.comment: Past simple would describe a finished past habit, but this sentence is about your routine now.

commonWrongAnswers.answer: I have gone to the gym every morning before work.
commonWrongAnswers.comment: Present perfect doesn't fit a simple routine with 'every morning'.

questions.context: Mr Evans has a bad cough. His doctor strongly advised him to give up smoking, and he finally decided to quit. He said: "I have stopped ___ cigarettes, so I feel much better." (smoke)
questions.instruction: Write the correct form of the verb in brackets.
questions.explanation: 'Stop' followed by -ing means you quit the activity, so it's 'stopped smoking'.

commonWrongAnswers.comment: After 'stop', 'to smoke' would mean he stopped something else in order to smoke, which isn't the meaning here.
The verb after 'stopped' needs a special form, not the base form.

questions.context: At the pharmacy, you must to show a prescription for this medicine.
questions.correctAnswer: At the pharmacy, you must show a prescription for this medicine.
questions.explanation: After a modal verb like 'must', we use the base verb without 'to'.

commonWrongAnswers.answer: At the pharmacy, you must showing a prescription for this medicine.
commonWrongAnswers.comment: A modal verb is followed by the base form, not an -ing form.

commonWrongAnswers.answer: At the pharmacy, you musts show a prescription for this medicine.
commonWrongAnswers.comment: Modal verbs never take an -s ending, whoever the subject is.
